subUnits.title: 3.1 Stage and Performance Terms
notes: Stage and Performance Terms
Key Concepts:
1. Speech Types:
- DIALOGUE: conversation between two or more characters — the primary mode of dramatic communication.
- SOLILOQUY: a speech by a character ALONE on stage, revealing inner thoughts to the audience (e.g., Hamlet's 'To be or not to be').
- ASIDE: a brief remark to the audience, unheard by other characters on stage.
- MONOLOGUE: an extended speech, possibly with others present (unlike soliloquy).
2. Production Terms:
- PROLOGUE: an introductory speech before the play begins.
- EPILOGUE: a closing speech at the end of the play.
- PROMPT: helping an actor recall forgotten lines during performance.
- SCRIPT: the written text of the play.
- DRAMATIS PERSONAE: the list of characters appearing in the play.
- MIME: performance through action without speech.
Analogy:

- A SOLILOQUY revealing a character's inner thoughts, alone on stage, is like reading someone's private DIARY: the audience gains access to what the character truly thinks, without other characters knowing.
Common Mistakes:
- Do NOT confuse ASIDE (brief, others present but unhearing) with SOLILOQUY (longer, character alone on stage).
- Do NOT confuse PROLOGUE (opening speech) with EPILOGUE (closing speech).

quiz.q: A soliloquy is:
opts: A conversation between two characters
A speech by a character alone on stage, revealing inner thoughts
A brief remark to the audience while others are present
The opening speech before the play begins
quiz.explanation: A soliloquy is delivered when the character is alone, allowing the audience to hear their unspoken thoughts.

quiz.q: An aside is:
opts: A long speech delivered alone on stage
The written text of the play
A brief remark to the audience, unheard by other characters
The list of characters in a play
quiz.explanation: An aside is a brief, quiet remark directed at the audience, which other characters on stage cannot hear.

quiz.q: How does a monologue differ from a soliloquy?
opts: A monologue is shorter than a soliloquy
A monologue may be delivered with others present; a soliloquy is delivered alone
A soliloquy is always happy; a monologue is always sad
There is no difference between them
quiz.explanation: The key distinction is context: a soliloquy requires the character to be alone; a monologue may occur with others present.

quiz.q: The 'Dramatis Personae' in a play refers to:
opts: The main conflict in the play
The list of characters appearing in the play
The stage directions for the opening scene
The title of the play
quiz.explanation: Dramatis personae (Latin: 'persons of the drama') is the list of all characters in a play.

quiz.q: A PROLOGUE occurs:
opts: At the very end of the play
In the middle of act two
Before the play begins
After the final scene
quiz.explanation: A prologue is an introductory speech delivered before the main action of the play begins.

quiz.q: An EPILOGUE occurs:
opts: Before the play begins
At the very end, after the main action concludes
During the climax of the play
Between acts one and two
quiz.explanation: An epilogue is a closing speech delivered at the end of the play.

quiz.q: The analogy comparing a soliloquy to reading someone's private diary illustrates:
opts: That soliloquies are always dishonest
That the audience gains access to the character's true, unguarded inner thoughts
That soliloquies are only written, never spoken
That all characters know what is said in a soliloquy
quiz.explanation: Like a diary, a soliloquy reveals what the character truly thinks — shared with the audience, hidden from other characters.

quiz.q: Mime in drama refers to:
opts: A form of dialogue using rapid speech
Performance through action without speech
A comic sub-plot
The script of a play
quiz.explanation: Mime conveys meaning entirely through physical action and movement, without words.

quiz.q: It is a mistake to confuse an aside with a soliloquy because:
opts: They are exactly the same thing
An aside is brief with others present; a soliloquy is longer with the character alone
A soliloquy is shorter than an aside
An aside can only be done by the villain
quiz.explanation: They differ in length and context: aside is brief with others on stage; soliloquy is extended and the character is alone.

quiz.q: A PROMPT during a performance means:
opts: The playwright's opening instructions
Helping an actor recall forgotten lines
The closing bow at curtain call
The stage crew moving scenery
quiz.explanation: To prompt an actor is to quietly supply a forgotten line during a live performance.

subUnits.title: 3.2 Plot, Character, and Structural Terms in Drama
notes: Plot, Character, and Structural Terms in Drama
Key Concepts:
1. Plot Terms:
- FLASHBACK: interrupting chronological order to recall earlier events.
- FORESHADOWING: hinting at events that will occur later in the play.
- CONFLICT: the struggle between opposing forces — the engine of drama.
- CLIMAX: the point of highest tension in the play.
- DENOUEMENT: the final resolution after the climax.
2. Character and Dramatic Terms:
- PROTAGONIST: the main character of the drama.
- ANTAGONIST: the character or force opposing the protagonist.
- FLAT character: a one-dimensional character with little development.
- ROUND character: a complex, fully developed character.
- STOCK character: a familiar type (e.g., the miser, the scheming villain).
- COMIC RELIEF: humour inserted to ease tension, even within tragedies.
- HAMARTIA: the protagonist's fatal flaw.
- PERIPETEIA: a sudden reversal of fortune.
- ANAGNORISIS: the moment of crucial recognition or discovery.
- CATHARSIS: the emotional release felt by the audience after witnessing a tragic downfall.
Common Mistakes:
- Do NOT confuse PROTAGONIST (main character) with ANTAGONIST (opposing force).
- Do NOT assume comic relief occurs only in comedies — it appears in tragedies too, easing tension.

quiz.q: The CLIMAX of a play is:
opts: The opening scene
The point of highest tension in the drama
The final resolution of all conflicts
The list of characters
quiz.explanation: The climax is the turning point — the moment of greatest dramatic intensity.

quiz.q: DENOUEMENT refers to:
opts: The opening conflict
The point of highest tension
The final resolution after the climax
A reversal of fortune
quiz.explanation: The denouement is the resolution following the climax, tying up the loose ends of the plot.

quiz.q: FLASHBACK is a technique that:
opts: Hints at future events
Interrupts chronological order to recall earlier events
Resolves the main conflict
Introduces the protagonist
quiz.explanation: A flashback disrupts chronological sequence to show events that happened before the current action.

quiz.q: FORESHADOWING in a drama means:
opts: Recalling past events
Hinting at events that will occur later in the play
Providing comic relief
Reversing the protagonist's fortune
quiz.explanation: Foreshadowing plants hints or clues about what will happen later in the drama.

quiz.q: CATHARSIS refers to:
opts: The protagonist's fatal flaw
The list of characters
The emotional release felt by the audience after witnessing a tragic downfall
A sudden reversal of fortune
quiz.explanation: Catharsis (from Aristotle) is the purging of emotions — particularly pity and fear — that the audience experiences at the end of a tragedy.

quiz.q: PERIPETEIA refers to:
opts: The moment of recognition
A sudden reversal of fortune experienced by the protagonist
Comic relief within a tragedy
The opening speech of a play
quiz.explanation: Peripeteia is the dramatic reversal of fortune — often when the protagonist's situation suddenly changes from good to bad.

quiz.q: ANAGNORISIS refers to:
opts: A reversal of fortune
The protagonist's fatal flaw
The moment a character discovers a crucial truth
The closing speech of a play
quiz.explanation: Anagnorisis is the moment of discovery or recognition — when a character learns something crucial that changes the situation.

quiz.q: A ROUND character is:
opts: A character with one defining trait
A familiar stereotype like a miser
A complex, fully developed character
A character who opposes the protagonist
quiz.explanation: Round characters are multi-dimensional and developed, capable of change and surprise.

quiz.q: Comic relief in drama functions to:
opts: End the play abruptly
Ease tension by introducing humour, even within a tragedy
Replace all serious content
Confuse the audience
quiz.explanation: Comic relief provides brief moments of humour that give the audience emotional respite from sustained dramatic tension.

quiz.q: It is a mistake to confuse protagonist with antagonist because:
opts: They are the same character
The protagonist is the main character; the antagonist is the opposing force
Only comedies have protagonists
The antagonist is always more interesting
quiz.explanation: The protagonist is the central character whose journey drives the story; the antagonist is the opposing force they struggle against.

subUnits.title: 3.3 Stage Types, Backstage Terms, and the Classical Unities
notes: Stage Types, Backstage Terms, and the Classical Unities
Key Concepts:
1. Stage Types:
- PROSCENIUM: audience faces the stage through an arch — the most traditional arrangement.
- THRUST: the stage extends into the audience on three sides.
- ARENA / Theatre-in-the-Round: audience surrounds the stage on all sides.
- BLACK BOX: a flexible, minimalist performance space.
2. Backstage Areas:
- GREEN ROOM: the rest area where actors wait when not performing.
- FLY SYSTEM: the ropes and pulleys used to lift and lower scenery.
- TRAP ROOM: the space directly beneath the stage, used for special effects and entrances.
3. The Classical Unities (from Aristotle's Poetics):
- Unity of ACTION: one main plot, without irrelevant subplots.
- Unity of PLACE: the action occurs in a single location.
- Unity of TIME: the action takes place within roughly one day.
Analogy:
- The classical unities restricting a play to one plot, place, and day are like a strict RECIPE with exactly three ingredients: the limitation itself forces a tightly focused, disciplined result.
Common Mistakes:
- Do NOT confuse PROSCENIUM (audience facing through an arch) with THRUST (stage extending into audience).
- Do NOT assume the classical unities apply to every play — they reflect a specific neoclassical tradition, not a universal rule.

quiz.q: In a PROSCENIUM theatre, the audience:
opts: Surrounds the stage on all sides
Sits on three sides of the stage
Faces the stage through an arch
Stands in a flexible open space
quiz.explanation: The proscenium is the traditional stage with a framing arch, with the audience facing the stage from one side.

quiz.q: A THRUST stage is one where:
opts: The audience sits in a flexible arrangement
The stage extends into the audience on three sides
The audience surrounds the stage on all sides
There is no stage — only an open space
quiz.explanation: A thrust stage projects out into the audience, allowing actors to be surrounded on three sides.

quiz.q: A THEATRE-IN-THE-ROUND arrangement means:
opts: The stage is raised behind an arch
The audience sits in front of the stage
The audience completely surrounds the acting area
The stage extends into the audience on three sides
quiz.explanation: Arena/Theatre-in-the-round places the audience in a circle around the central performance space.

quiz.q: The GREEN ROOM in a theatre is:
opts: The space beneath the stage for special effects
The area where actors wait when not performing
The ropes and pulleys for lifting scenery
The costume wardrobe
quiz.explanation: The green room is the backstage rest area where performers wait between scenes.

quiz.q: The FLY SYSTEM in a theatre refers to:
opts: The actor's costume design
The audience seating arrangement
The ropes and pulleys used to raise and lower scenery
The trap room beneath the stage
quiz.explanation: The fly system is the technical rigging above the stage used to fly scenery and props in and out of view.

quiz.q: The Unity of Action (from Aristotle) requires:
opts: The play to last exactly one day
A single location for all events
One main plot, without irrelevant subplots
All characters to be present throughout
quiz.explanation: Unity of action demands that the drama follow one central storyline without distraction from irrelevant subplots.

quiz.q: The Unity of Time requires that:
opts: The action occurs in a single location
The action spans no more than roughly one day
There is only one character
The play is performed without intervals
quiz.explanation: Unity of time limits the dramatic action to a single day (or approximately so).

quiz.q: The Unity of Place requires that:
opts: The action occurs in a single location
The play lasts one day
There is only one protagonist
The stage has no props
quiz.explanation: Unity of place demands that all dramatic action occurs in one location.

quiz.q: It is a mistake to assume the classical unities apply to every play because:
opts: No plays follow any rules
They reflect a specific neoclassical tradition, not a universal rule for all drama
The unities were invented after most plays were written
Only Greek plays must follow the unities
quiz.explanation: The classical unities are a neoclassical ideal, not an absolute rule — many celebrated plays deliberately break them.

quiz.q: A BLACK BOX theatre is characterised by:
opts: A fixed proscenium arch with formal seating
A flexible, minimalist performance space
An arena with the audience surrounding the stage
A thrust stage extending into the audience
quiz.explanation: The black box is a versatile, bare space that can be configured in multiple ways for different productions.
